result:
There's a particular kind of vertigo that comes from reading about dark matter. Everything we can see—every star, every galaxy, every person and planet—accounts for roughly five percent of the universe. The rest is stuff we cannot touch, cannot see, and still cannot fully explain. We named it "dark" not because we know its color, but because we were describing our own ignorance with the only word we had left.

I find this oddly comforting rather than frightening. It means the universe has kept some of its secrets despite centuries of telescopes, equations, and stubborn human attention. There is still wilderness. Not the kind you hike through, but the kind you think your way into—the unmapped interior of reality itself.

It also suggests something humbling about certainty. The people who were sure the Milky Way was the entire universe were wrong. The people who were sure atoms were indivisible were wrong. Being wrong at scale seems to be how science breathes; each confident error becomes the doorway to the next room.

So maybe the right posture toward existence isn't mastery but attentiveness. Notice things. Ask small questions. Great discoveries rarely announce themselves—they hide in odd details: an unexplained orbit, a faint background hum, a measurement that refuses to come out clean no matter how many times you repeat it.

Five percent visible. Ninety-five percent mystery. Honestly, that ratio feels about right for a universe worth living in—a place large enough to keep us curious, and strange enough to keep us honest.
